title: Algorithm Design
subject: Algorithms
cue: Asked whether a procedure always returns the required result.
theory: Separate correctness, termination and resource use. A fast procedure can still be incorrect.
For a loop proof, establish the invariant initially, preserve it for one iteration, and combine it with termination.

recall.q: What are the three stages of a loop-invariant proof?
recall.a: Initialization, maintenance, termination.

pitfall: Testing a few examples can disprove correctness, but cannot prove correctness for every input.

title: Algorithm Design Techniques
subject: Algorithms
cue: Asked which design technique suits a problem.
theory: Divide and conquer solves smaller instances and combines results; dynamic programming stores answers to overlapping states.
A greedy choice needs a correctness argument, often an exchange argument or a cut property.

recall.q: What distinguishes dynamic programming from ordinary divide and conquer?
recall.a: DP reuses overlapping subproblem results; ordinary divide and conquer generally has independent subproblems.

pitfall: Optimal substructure alone does not justify a greedy algorithm.

title: Asymptotic Notation
subject: Algorithms
cue: Compare growth rates, bounds or nested logarithms.
theory: O(g) is an asymptotic upper bound; Ω(g) is a lower bound; Θ(g) means both bounds hold.
For positive functions, a finite nonzero limit of f(n)/g(n) establishes Θ; limit zero establishes little-o.

recall.q: Does f(n)=O(n²) mean f must take quadratic time?
recall.a: No. Linear and constant functions are also O(n²); Θ is the tight-growth claim.

pitfall: Big-O does not itself mean worst case; it can bound any specified cost function.

title: Bellman–Ford
subject: Algorithms
cue: Shortest paths with negative edge weights.
theory: Bellman–Ford repeatedly relaxes all edges; after k full passes, paths using at most k edges are accounted for.
With no reachable negative cycle, V−1 passes suffice. A further improvement signals a reachable negative cycle.

recall.q: What is Bellman–Ford’s standard running time?
recall.a: O(VE).

pitfall: A negative cycle outside the source’s reachable region does not invalidate source distances.

title: Binary Heap
subject: Algorithms
cue: Priority-based selection or heap operations.
theory: A binary heap is complete and obeys parent–child heap order; unrelated siblings need not be sorted.
Bottom-up construction is Θ(n); inserting or extracting a root is O(log n).

recall.q: Why is building a heap not necessarily Θ(n log n)?
recall.a: Most nodes are near the leaves and need little or no downward work; summing work by height gives Θ(n).

pitfall: A heap is not a binary search tree.

title: Binary Search
subject: Algorithms
cue: Sorted input or a monotone yes/no condition.
theory: Binary search maintains an interval that contains the target and discards about half each step.
On an indexed sorted array, comparisons are O(log n); choose consistent inclusive or half-open bounds.

recall.q: What condition makes binary search on an answer possible?
recall.a: A monotone feasibility predicate, so all infeasible and feasible candidates form ordered regions.

pitfall: Searching a linked list does not provide constant-time access to its middle.

title: Binary Search Trees
subject: Algorithms
cue: Search paths or order queries in a BST.
theory: For distinct keys, left-subtree keys are smaller and right-subtree keys are larger than the node key.
Search, insert and delete cost O(h), where h is tree height; h can be n−1 in an unbalanced BST.

recall.q: What order does inorder traversal of a BST produce?
recall.a: Sorted key order.

pitfall: O(log n) requires a height guarantee or an average-case assumption.

title: Binary Trees
subject: Algorithms
cue: Tree shapes, leaf counts or height bounds.
theory: With root depth 0, a binary tree has at most 2ᵈ nodes at depth d and at most 2ʰ⁺¹−1 nodes through height h.
For a nonempty binary tree, the number of leaves equals the number of two-child nodes plus one.

recall.q: Does a binary tree require every node to have two children?
recall.a: No; each node has at most two children. A full/proper binary tree requires zero or two.

pitfall: Complete, full and perfect are different tree properties.

title: Breadth-First Search
subject: Algorithms
cue: Minimum number of edges from a source.
theory: BFS uses a queue and discovers vertices in nondecreasing distance from the source.
With adjacency lists it takes O(V+E); predecessor edges give a shortest-path tree in an unweighted graph.

recall.q: When is BFS a shortest-path algorithm?
recall.a: When edges are unweighted or all have the same weight.

pitfall: Different adjacency orders may give different valid BFS trees.

title: Bubble Sort
subject: Algorithms
cue: Repeated adjacent comparisons and swaps.
theory: Bubble sort swaps adjacent out-of-order elements; each pass can place a largest remaining key.
Worst-case time is Θ(n²). An early-exit flag gives Θ(n) best case on already sorted input.

recall.q: What does the number of adjacent swaps equal when sorting distinct keys?
recall.a: The initial inversion count.

pitfall: Without early termination, even sorted input can take quadratic comparisons.

title: Master Theorem: Additional Practice
subject: Algorithms
cue: A recurrence has the form aT(n/b)+f(n).
theory: Compare f(n) with n^(log_b a). For f(n)=Θ(n^(log_b a)), the basic theorem gives Θ(n^(log_b a) log n).
The polynomial-gap cases require their stated conditions; the large-f case also needs a regularity condition. Use a recursion tree when the theorem does not apply.

recall.q: What is T(n)=2T(n/2)+n, with constant-size base cases?
recall.a: Θ(n log n).

pitfall: The source item is labeled GATE CS Practice, not an actual exam PYQ. Its “Computer Science” label is too broad.

correction.original: The source category is labeled “Computer Science”.
correction.corrected: The single item is Master-theorem practice and should be labeled separately from exam PYQs.
correction.reason: Its heading explicitly says GATE CS Practice: The Master Theorem and gives no exam year/question number.

title: Depth-First Search
subject: Algorithms
cue: DFS times, back edges, cycles or finishing order.
theory: DFS follows one path deeply before backtracking. A visited set prevents repeated expansion.
With adjacency lists, DFS costs O(V+E); reverse finish order gives a topological order in a DAG.

recall.q: What does a back edge indicate in directed DFS?
recall.a: A directed cycle.

pitfall: Do not apply directed-edge classifications to undirected graphs without accounting for the parent edge.

title: Dijkstra’s Algorithm
subject: Algorithms
cue: Weighted shortest paths with nonnegative edges.
theory: Dijkstra repeatedly finalizes an unsettled vertex with smallest tentative distance and relaxes its outgoing edges.
A binary heap with adjacency lists gives O((V+E) log V); a simple array implementation can take O(V²).

recall.q: Why do negative edges threaten Dijkstra’s greedy step?
recall.a: A later path through an unsettled vertex may reduce a distance already finalized.

pitfall: Dijkstra constructs shortest paths, not a minimum spanning tree.

title: Directed Acyclic Graphs
subject: Algorithms
cue: Dependencies, topological orders or paths in an acyclic digraph.
theory: A directed graph has a topological ordering exactly when it has no directed cycle.
Process a DAG in topological order to relax edges for shortest or longest paths, including negative weights.

recall.q: Can a DAG have negative-weight edges?
recall.a: Yes; it has no cycles, so no negative cycles.

pitfall: A topological ordering need not be unique.

title: Double Hashing
subject: Algorithms
cue: An open-address probe sequence uses two hashes.
theory: Double hashing probes (h₁(k)+i·h₂(k)) mod m for i=0,1,….
The step h₂(k) must be nonzero and coprime to m to visit every slot.

recall.q: For prime table size m, which step sizes visit all slots?
recall.a: Any integer from 1 to m−1.

pitfall: A zero step or a common factor with m can trap probing in a subset of slots.

title: Dynamic Programming
subject: Algorithms
cue: Repeated subproblems and an optimum over choices.
theory: Define a state by all information needed for future decisions, then a recurrence and base cases.
Memoization is top-down caching; tabulation is bottom-up evaluation in dependency order.

recall.q: How do you estimate DP running time?
recall.a: Number of reachable states × work per state, including the transitions examined.

pitfall: A recurrence without clear state meaning is easy to index incorrectly.

title: Graph Algorithms
subject: Algorithms
cue: Choose an algorithm from graph constraints.
theory: BFS handles unweighted distances; Dijkstra handles nonnegative weights; Bellman–Ford handles negative edges.
DFS/BFS test reachability; Kruskal/Prim connect an undirected graph with minimum total tree weight.

recall.q: What separates a shortest-path tree from an MST?
recall.a: A shortest-path tree minimizes source-to-vertex distances; an MST minimizes total selected edge weight.

pitfall: Check directed versus undirected and weighted versus unweighted before choosing a method.

title: Graph Traversal and Search
subject: Algorithms
cue: Possible traversal orders or graph-search forests.
theory: A graph traversal may need a new start vertex after each disconnected component.
BFS uses a queue; iterative DFS uses a stack; recursive DFS uses the call stack.

recall.q: Why might one source fail to visit every vertex?
recall.a: The graph can have disconnected or unreachable vertices.

pitfall: A traversal tree contains discovery edges, not every original graph edge.

title: Greedy Algorithms
subject: Algorithms
cue: Choose the locally best remaining option.
theory: A greedy algorithm commits to a choice without revisiting it. Prove that some optimal solution can include that choice.
For interval scheduling by maximum count, earliest finishing time is a correct greedy rule.

recall.q: What should follow a proposed greedy rule?
recall.a: A proof such as an exchange argument, or a counterexample showing it fails.

pitfall: A rule that works for fractional knapsack need not work for 0/1 knapsack.

title: Hashing
subject: Algorithms
cue: Collisions, load factor or expected probes.
theory: Load factor α=n/m is stored keys divided by table slots. Separate chaining may have α>1; open addressing requires free slots.
Expected O(1) operations require suitable hashing and controlled load, not merely the presence of a hash function.

recall.q: What is a collision?
recall.a: Two different keys obtain the same initial table index.

pitfall: Hashing does not guarantee O(1) worst-case lookup.

title: Heapsort
subject: Algorithms
cue: In-place sorting through repeated maximum removal.
theory: Build a max-heap, swap its root to the end, shrink the heap, and restore heap order.
Standard heapsort is O(n log n) worst case with O(1) auxiliary array space, and is generally unstable.

recall.q: Which heap is used for increasing-order heapsort?
recall.a: A max-heap.

pitfall: Heap order alone does not mean the array is fully sorted.

title: Huffman Coding
subject: Algorithms
cue: Minimum weighted code length for symbol frequencies.
theory: Huffman coding repeatedly merges the two smallest weights; merged nodes become an internal tree node.
Weighted code length is Σ fᵢ·lᵢ, also equal to the sum of all merge weights.

recall.q: Why can a prefix code be decoded unambiguously?
recall.a: No codeword is the prefix of another, so reaching a leaf determines a symbol.

pitfall: Ties can yield different optimal codes with the same total cost.

title: Identify a Function from Code
subject: Algorithms
cue: A code fragment asks “what function does this compute?”
theory: Trace several small inputs, identify what each variable means, and infer a loop or recursion invariant.
Write a mathematical expression for the returned value; separately account for mutation and output side effects.

recall.q: What is the first move when identifying an unfamiliar recursive function?
recall.a: Check base cases, then express its result in terms of smaller calls.

pitfall: The source label “Identify Function” means infer code behavior, not the identity function f(x)=x.

correction.original: The note treats “Identify Function” as an identity function.
correction.corrected: This source category asks readers to infer what supplied program code computes.
correction.reason: The actual questions on pages 56–68 ask for outputs and mathematical behavior of code, not properties of f(x)=x.

title: Insertion Sort
subject: Algorithms
cue: Sorted prefix grows one inserted key at a time.
theory: Insertion sort places each next key within the already sorted prefix.
Standard insertion sort is stable and in-place; best case Θ(n), worst case Θ(n²), with work tied to inversions.

recall.q: Why is insertion sort useful on nearly sorted data?
recall.a: There are few inversions, so few shifts are required.

pitfall: Binary-searching the insertion position reduces comparisons, but array shifts can still be quadratic.

title: Inversions
subject: Algorithms
cue: Count pairs out of sorted order.
theory: An inversion is a pair i<j with A[i]>A[j]. Distinct reverse-sorted keys have n(n−1)/2 inversions.
Count cross-half inversions while merging to obtain an O(n log n) algorithm.

recall.q: How many inversions does one adjacent out-of-order swap remove?
recall.a: Exactly one.

pitfall: Equal keys are not inversions under the strict greater-than definition.

title: Linear Probing
subject: Algorithms
cue: Collisions resolved by checking consecutive slots.
theory: Linear probing uses (h(k)+i) mod m. Contiguous occupied blocks cause primary clustering.
Search follows the insertion probe sequence; deletion needs a tombstone or rehashing to preserve search paths.

recall.q: Why can clearing a deleted slot break lookup?
recall.a: A later key in the same probe chain may become unreachable when lookup stops at the cleared slot.

pitfall: Wrap from the final table index back to zero.

title: Matrix-Chain Multiplication
subject: Algorithms
cue: Choose parenthesization of a matrix product.
theory: For dimensions p₀×p₁,…,pₙ₋₁×pₙ, m[i,j]=minₖ(m[i,k]+m[k+1,j]+pᵢ₋₁pₖpⱼ).
Set m[i,i]=0 and fill by increasing chain length; the standard DP uses O(n³) time and O(n²) space.

recall.q: Does matrix-chain ordering change the order of the matrices?
recall.a: No; it changes parenthesization only.

pitfall: The merge cost uses the outer dimensions of the two product matrices.

title: Minimum and Maximum
subject: Algorithms
cue: Minimum comparisons to find both extremes.
theory: Finding one extreme among n distinct numbers requires n−1 comparisons in the comparison model.
Pairing elements first finds both minimum and maximum in ⌈3n/2⌉−2 comparisons for n≥2.

recall.q: Why pair numbers before finding min and max?
recall.a: Only pair winners compete for maximum and pair losers for minimum.

pitfall: Do not assume independently finding both extremes is optimal.

title: Merge Sort
subject: Algorithms
cue: Recursively sort halves, then merge.
theory: Merge sort satisfies T(n)=2T(n/2)+Θ(n), hence Θ(n log n).
Standard array merge sort uses Θ(n) auxiliary storage and is stable if ties are taken from the left run first.

recall.q: What is the maximum number of comparisons to merge sizes a and b?
recall.a: a+b−1 when both are nonempty.

pitfall: Time and auxiliary space are separate quantities.

title: Merging Sorted Sequences
subject: Algorithms
cue: Combine sorted sequences or choose merge order.
theory: Two sorted arrays of lengths a and b can be merged in Θ(a+b) time.
For minimum total binary-merge cost, repeatedly merging the two smallest file sizes is the optimal-merge pattern.

recall.q: What determines the cost of one full merge?
recall.a: The combined lengths of the input runs.

pitfall: Concatenating two sorted lists does not generally produce a sorted list.

title: Minimum Spanning Trees
subject: Algorithms
cue: Connect every vertex with minimum total edge weight.
theory: An MST of a connected undirected graph has V−1 edges. A minimum edge across any cut is safe for some MST.
An edge strictly heavier than every other edge on a cycle cannot belong to an MST.

recall.q: Do distinct edge weights imply a unique MST?
recall.a: Yes. The converse is not required: some graphs with repeated weights also have a unique MST.

pitfall: A light edge tied with others is not necessarily in every MST.

title: Counting Swaps
subject: Algorithms
cue: Minimum swaps to sort an arrangement.
theory: For distinct keys, unrestricted swaps to sort a permutation equal n minus its number of cycles, including fixed points.
If only adjacent swaps are allowed, the minimum is the inversion count.

recall.q: What information must you check before applying a swap formula?
recall.a: Whether swaps may exchange arbitrary positions or only adjacent positions.

pitfall: Repeated keys can require choosing a target matching; the distinct-key cycle formula needs care.

title: Prim’s Algorithm
subject: Algorithms
cue: Grow one minimum-cost tree across a cut.
theory: Prim repeatedly adds a lightest edge from the current tree to a vertex outside it.
It accepts negative edge weights; a heap-based adjacency-list implementation takes O(E log V).

recall.q: What does Prim’s key for a vertex represent?
recall.a: The weight of its lightest known edge connecting it to the current tree.

pitfall: Prim’s key is not the total path distance from the starting vertex.

title: Quicksort
subject: Algorithms
cue: Partition around a pivot.
theory: Quicksort recursively sorts the partitions. Balanced splits give Θ(n log n); consistently extreme pivots can give Θ(n²).
Random pivots give expected Θ(n log n); recursive stack space depends on partition balance and implementation.

recall.q: What recurrence describes repeated one-versus-n−1 splits?
recall.a: T(n)=T(n−1)+Θ(n), giving Θ(n²).

pitfall: Expected good performance is not a worst-case guarantee.

title: Recurrence Relations
subject: Algorithms
cue: Recursive running-time equation.
theory: For T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n), compare f(n) with n^(log_b a) and check the applicable Master-theorem conditions.
Use substitution, a recursion tree or telescoping when the recurrence does not fit the theorem.

recall.q: Why can’t the basic Master theorem directly solve T(n)=T(n−1)+n?
recall.a: Its subproblem must shrink by a constant factor n/b, not by subtraction.

pitfall: Include the number of recursive calls and the nonrecursive work.

title: Recursion
subject: Algorithms
cue: Count calls, depth or work of recursive code.
theory: Recursion depth measures the longest active call chain; total calls count every node in the call tree.
Stack space is based on simultaneously active frames, not the total number of calls.

recall.q: Can exponential total calls use only linear stack depth?
recall.a: Yes, a binary recursion of depth n can have exponentially many calls but O(n) active frames.

pitfall: Separate call count, work per call and maximum depth.

title: Searching
subject: Algorithms
cue: Locate a key under given storage constraints.
theory: Linear search needs O(n) comparisons in the worst case and does not require ordering.
Binary search needs sorted, efficiently indexed data and takes O(log n) comparisons.

recall.q: What extra structure enables binary search?
recall.a: A sorted or monotone search space and efficient access to chosen middle positions.

pitfall: A cost for sorting the input cannot be ignored unless it is already sorted.

title: Selection Sort
subject: Algorithms
cue: Repeatedly select the smallest remaining key.
theory: Selection sort performs n(n−1)/2 key comparisons in its standard form regardless of initial order.
It uses O(1) auxiliary array space and O(n) swaps, but the usual swap-based form is not stable.

recall.q: Does sorted input reduce standard selection-sort comparisons?
recall.a: No; it still searches the remaining suffix each pass.

pitfall: Few swaps do not imply few comparisons.

title: Shortest Paths
subject: Algorithms
cue: Minimum path cost between vertices.
theory: A shortest-path problem minimizes total weight along a path, not the number of edges unless weights are equal.
A reachable negative cycle that can lead to a destination makes its shortest-walk cost unbounded below.

recall.q: Which algorithm handles all-pairs shortest paths in O(V³)?
recall.a: Floyd–Warshall.

pitfall: A negative edge is not the same as a negative cycle.

title: Sorting
subject: Algorithms
cue: Compare sorting guarantees, stability or lower bounds.
theory: General comparison sorting requires Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. Counting/radix sorts use assumptions beyond arbitrary comparison.
Stability preserves the original relative order of equal keys; in-place concerns auxiliary storage.

recall.q: Why does linear-time counting sort not contradict the comparison lower bound?
recall.a: It uses key values and a bounded range, not only comparisons.

pitfall: Check the range/base assumptions in noncomparison sorting.

title: Space Complexity
subject: Algorithms
cue: Memory used by variables, data structures or recursion.
theory: Auxiliary space excludes the input unless the problem defines otherwise.
For recursive code, sum memory along the deepest simultaneously active call chain.

recall.q: What is the stack space of recursive binary search?
recall.a: O(log n); the iterative version can use O(1) auxiliary space.

pitfall: Total allocations over time are not necessarily peak live memory.

title: Strongly Connected Components
subject: Algorithms
cue: Mutual reachability in a directed graph.
theory: An SCC is a maximal set in which every vertex reaches every other vertex.
Contracting SCCs produces a DAG; Kosaraju and Tarjan run in O(V+E) with adjacency lists.

recall.q: Can the condensation graph contain a directed cycle?
recall.a: No; a cycle of components would merge into one SCC.

pitfall: Weak connectivity ignores edge direction and is different.

title: Time Complexity
subject: Algorithms
cue: Count how many times an operation executes.
theory: Translate dependent loop bounds into a sum; do not multiply maxima when inner work depends on the outer index.
A variable multiplied or divided by a fixed factor typically contributes logarithmic iterations.

recall.q: What is 1+2+…+n asymptotically?
recall.a: Θ(n²).

pitfall: An apparent nesting of two loops does not always imply Θ(n²).

title: Topological Sorting
subject: Algorithms
cue: Order jobs subject to prerequisites.
theory: A topological order places u before v for every directed edge u→v.
Kahn’s algorithm repeatedly removes zero-indegree vertices; failure to remove all vertices reveals a cycle.

recall.q: When is the topological order unique in Kahn’s method?
recall.a: When exactly one zero-indegree choice is available at every step.

pitfall: A disconnected DAG can have many valid interleavings.

title: Tree Traversals
subject: Algorithms
cue: Reconstruct or compare traversal sequences.
theory: Preorder is node–left–right, inorder is left–node–right, postorder is left–right–node.
For distinct keys, inorder plus preorder or postorder uniquely identifies a binary tree.

recall.q: Do preorder and postorder always uniquely determine a binary tree?
recall.a: No; a single-child subtree can be ambiguous.

pitfall: A binary tree need not be a BST.

title: Uniform Hashing
subject: Algorithms
cue: Expected probes under an explicit random-hashing model.
theory: Simple uniform hashing distributes keys evenly over buckets; open-address uniform hashing assumes probe permutations are equally likely.
For open addressing at load α<1, the classic unsuccessful-search bound is 1/(1−α).

recall.q: What happens to expected open-address probes as α approaches 1?
recall.a: They rise sharply because few slots remain empty.

pitfall: Uniform hashing is a model assumption, not a property guaranteed by every hash function.

title: Abstract Syntax Trees
subject: Compiler Design
cue: Represent expression structure without grammar scaffolding.
theory: An AST keeps operators and meaningful operands while omitting syntactic details such as parentheses and many grammar nonterminals.
An expression DAG may share a node for an identical reusable subexpression; a tree represents each occurrence separately.

recall.q: How does an AST differ from a parse tree?
recall.a: The parse tree records grammar derivation; the AST keeps the essential program structure.

pitfall: An AST node count is not generally the parse-tree node count.

title: Grammar Ambiguity
subject: Compiler Design
cue: A sentence has multiple possible structures.
theory: A CFG is ambiguous if some string has two different parse trees, equivalently two distinct leftmost derivations.
Operator precedence and associativity can often be encoded by rewriting an expression grammar.

recall.q: Do two different arbitrary derivation orders prove ambiguity?
recall.a: No. Independent nonterminals may be expanded in different orders yet yield the same tree.

pitfall: An ambiguous grammar does not imply the language is inherently ambiguous.

title: Assemblers
subject: Compiler Design
cue: Resolve symbolic labels into addresses in assembly code.
theory: A two-pass assembler first assigns addresses and builds a symbol table, then emits code while resolving references.
Relocation adjusts address-dependent fields when code is placed at a different load address.

recall.q: Why is a second assembler pass useful?
recall.a: It resolves forward references whose label addresses were unknown at first use.

pitfall: An assembler translates assembly; it does not perform high-level parsing like a C compiler.

title: Backpatching
subject: Compiler Design
cue: Generate jumps before their targets are known.
theory: Backpatching keeps lists of incomplete jump instructions and fills their target fields when the destination is known.
Short-circuit Boolean translation often uses truelist, falselist and nextlist.

recall.q: What does backpatch(list, target) do?
recall.a: It fills the missing target of every jump in the list with target.

pitfall: The list contains instruction positions needing targets, not the target labels themselves.

title: Basic Blocks and Flow Graphs
subject: Compiler Design
cue: Split three-address code into straight-line regions.
theory: A basic block has one entry and no branching except possibly its last instruction.
Leaders include the first instruction, jump targets, and the instruction immediately following a jump.

recall.q: Why is a jump target a basic-block leader?
recall.a: Execution may enter there without executing preceding instructions.

pitfall: A label that is a possible entry cannot lie in the middle of the same block.

title: Code Optimization
subject: Compiler Design
cue: Eliminate redundant computation without changing meaning.
theory: Constant folding evaluates constant expressions; constant propagation substitutes known constant values; dead-code elimination removes work with no observable effect.
Common-subexpression elimination reuses a value only if the operands have not changed and side effects permit reuse.

recall.q: When can x+y be reused later?
recall.a: When the relevant values of x and y are unchanged and the operation can safely be reused.

pitfall: Pointer aliases, function calls and volatile accesses can block apparently safe optimization.

title: Compilation Phases
subject: Compiler Design
cue: Match an error or task with a compiler phase.
theory: Lexical analysis forms tokens; parsing checks syntax; semantic analysis checks meaning such as types and declarations.
Intermediate code is optimized and translated to target code; symbol information can support several phases.

recall.q: Which phase distinguishes a token such as identifier from a sequence of characters?
recall.a: Lexical analysis.

pitfall: A pass is an implementation traversal; a phase is a conceptual task.

title: Tokenization
subject: Compiler Design
cue: Count tokens in a source fragment.
theory: A token has a category and optional attribute; its lexeme is the actual character sequence in the program.
Whitespace and comments usually separate tokens but are not ordinary parser tokens themselves.

recall.q: Are the identifier lexemes count and total the same token category?
recall.a: Yes; both are identifiers, with different attributes or lexemes.

pitfall: Multi-character operators such as <= are one token under the language’s lexical rules.

title: DAGs for Basic Blocks
subject: Compiler Design
cue: Find shared computations inside a basic block.
theory: A DAG for a basic block represents values and operations, sharing identical computations when operands refer to the same values.
After an assignment changes a variable, later uses may refer to a new value node.

recall.q: Can two textual occurrences of a+b always share a DAG node?
recall.a: No; a or b may have been redefined between them.

pitfall: Track values, not just variable spellings.

title: Expression Evaluation
subject: Compiler Design
cue: Evaluate expression trees or generated instructions.
theory: A tree’s structure fixes which operands belong to each operator; precedence and associativity determine that structure.
For pure arithmetic, different evaluation orders may compute the same value but use different registers.

recall.q: Does left associativity force every operand to be evaluated left to right?
recall.a: No. Grouping and evaluation order are separate language rules.

pitfall: Side effects can make evaluation order observable.

title: FIRST and FOLLOW
subject: Compiler Design
cue: Compute predictive-parsing entries or nullable sequences.
theory: FIRST(α) contains terminals that can begin strings derived from α, and ε when α is nullable.
FOLLOW(A) contains terminals that may follow A; include end marker for the start symbol and propagate through nullable suffixes.

recall.q: When adding a production A→α to an LL(1) table, what if ε is in FIRST(α)?
recall.a: Add that production under symbols in FOLLOW(A), as well as its non-ε FIRST terminals.

pitfall: ε is not a member of a FOLLOW set.

title: Grammar Analysis
subject: Compiler Design
cue: Derivations, grammar transformations or parse properties.
theory: A CFG production replaces one nonterminal by a string of terminals and nonterminals.
Left factoring delays a choice; eliminating left recursion enables common top-down parsing constructions but need not remove ambiguity.

recall.q: Does eliminating left recursion guarantee LL(1)?
recall.a: No. FIRST/FIRST or FIRST/FOLLOW conflicts can remain.

pitfall: Grammar transformation may change parse-tree structure while preserving the language.

title: Intermediate Code
subject: Compiler Design
cue: Convert expressions or control flow into a low-level representation.
theory: Three-address code breaks expressions into small operations using temporaries, assignments, branches and labels.
Quadruples record operator, two arguments and result; triples refer to instruction positions for intermediate results.

recall.q: Why introduce temporary variables in intermediate code?
recall.a: They make each step explicit and separate source syntax from target-machine details.

pitfall: A complex expression usually needs several three-address instructions.

title: LR SLR and LALR Parsing
subject: Compiler Design
cue: LR items, lookaheads, conflicts or parser hierarchy.
theory: LR parsing reads left to right and constructs a rightmost derivation in reverse by shift/reduce actions.
SLR uses FOLLOW sets for reductions; canonical LR(1) uses item-specific lookaheads; LALR merges LR(1) states with equal LR(0) cores.

recall.q: Can LALR merging introduce a reduce/reduce conflict?
recall.a: Yes, even when the canonical LR(1) table has none.

pitfall: LR(1) is a grammar property; a failed SLR table does not prove the grammar is not LR(1).

title: Lexical Analysis
subject: Compiler Design
cue: Recognize token patterns or resolve competing matches.
theory: Regular expressions describe token patterns and finite automata implement recognition.
Common lexers choose the longest match, then rule priority for equal-length matches.

recall.q: Which wins between keyword if and identifier rules on the lexeme if?
recall.a: With equal length, the lexer’s rule priority decides; keyword rules are commonly prioritized.

pitfall: A lexer recognizes tokens; balanced nesting generally belongs to the parser.

title: Linking and Relocation
subject: Compiler Design
cue: Combine object modules or resolve external symbols.
theory: A linker combines object files, resolves external references and performs required relocation.
A loader maps the executable into memory; dynamic linking may defer some symbol resolution.

recall.q: Which tool resolves a function defined in another object module?
recall.a: The linker, or dynamic linker when resolution is deferred.

pitfall: Compile-time symbol tables and link-time external-symbol resolution are different stages.

title: Live Variable Analysis
subject: Compiler Design
cue: Determine whether a current value may be used later.
theory: A variable is live at a point if some path reaches a use of its current value before a redefinition.
Liveness is backward: OUT[B]=union of IN over successors; IN[B]=USE[B] ∪ (OUT[B]−DEF[B]).

recall.q: Why is union used over successor liveness sets?
recall.a: A use on any feasible successor path can make a value live.

pitfall: An assignment defines a new value; it does not necessarily make its old value live.

title: LL(1) Parsing
subject: Compiler Design
cue: Top-down predictive parsing with one lookahead.
theory: LL(1) reads left to right and produces a leftmost derivation using one lookahead token.
Alternatives for one nonterminal must have disjoint applicable prediction sets, accounting for ε and FOLLOW.

recall.q: What does a multiply filled LL(1) table cell show?
recall.a: The given grammar is not LL(1).

pitfall: An equivalent rewritten grammar may be LL(1) even when the original is not.

title: Macros
subject: Compiler Design
cue: Expansion substitutes text before later compilation.
theory: A macro expands its definition at use sites; function-like macros can evaluate an argument multiple times.
Parenthesize substituted arguments and the whole expression to avoid precedence surprises.

recall.q: Why can a macro SQUARE(i++) be dangerous?
recall.a: A typical expansion repeats i++, causing repeated side effects and potentially undefined behavior.

pitfall: A macro is not a normal function call with one evaluation per argument.

title: Operator Precedence
subject: Compiler Design
cue: Resolve which operator groups more tightly or reduce an operator-precedence handle.
theory: Precedence controls grouping between different operators; associativity controls grouping among equal-precedence operators.
Traditional operator-precedence parsing requires an appropriate operator grammar and conflict-free precedence relations.

recall.q: How does left associativity group a−b−c?
recall.a: As (a−b)−c.

pitfall: Parentheses override precedence; grouping does not by itself specify evaluation order.

title: Parameter Passing
subject: Compiler Design
cue: Compare call-by-value, reference or name.
theory: Call by value copies an argument value; call by reference binds the formal parameter to the caller’s variable.
Call by name reevaluates the argument expression in the caller’s environment when used, which can behave differently from reference.

recall.q: Does changing a value parameter change the caller’s variable?
recall.a: No, unless the copied value provides access to shared mutable storage, such as a pointer.

pitfall: Apply the passing mechanism stated in the question; C itself passes arguments by value.

title: Parsing
subject: Compiler Design
cue: Trace stack/input actions or identify a handle.
theory: Top-down parsing expands from the start symbol; bottom-up parsing reduces substrings toward it.
A handle is a production occurrence whose reduction is one step in reversing a rightmost derivation.

recall.q: What is a shift/reduce conflict?
recall.a: The parser table permits both shifting the next token and reducing a production in the same situation.

pitfall: Not every substring matching a production RHS is the correct handle.

title: Register Allocation
subject: Compiler Design
cue: Assign simultaneously needed values to registers.
theory: Construct an interference graph with edges between values that must coexist in registers.
A valid k-coloring assigns at most k registers; values that cannot fit may be spilled to memory.

recall.q: What does an interference edge mean?
recall.a: Its two values cannot share the same register at that time.

pitfall: The maximum number of live values is a lower bound; graph-coloring structure can require more registers.

title: Runtime Environments and Activation Records
subject: Compiler Design
cue: Activation records, recursion or access to nonlocals.
theory: Each active call may have an activation record with parameters, locals, saved state and a return address.
A dynamic/control link points to the caller; a static/access link follows lexical nesting to reach nonlocal variables.

recall.q: Which link helps find a variable in a lexically enclosing function?
recall.a: The static/access link, or an equivalent display mechanism.

pitfall: The caller need not be the lexical parent.

title: Static Single Assignment
subject: Compiler Design
cue: Each variable name is assigned once.
theory: SSA gives each definition a distinct name. A φ-function at a join selects the version corresponding to the incoming control-flow edge.
SSA makes def-use relationships explicit and supports propagation and optimization.

recall.q: Does a φ-function average or combine its inputs arithmetically?
recall.a: No; it selects the value from the predecessor path actually taken.

pitfall: A loop may need φ-functions despite a single assignment per SSA name.

title: Symbol Tables
subject: Compiler Design
cue: Track identifiers, scopes, types or storage information.
theory: A symbol table maps declared names to information such as type, scope and storage location.
Nested scopes require shadowing rules, often represented by scoped tables or a stack of environments.

recall.q: Can the same spelling have several symbol-table entries?
recall.a: Yes, when different declarations occur in different scopes.

pitfall: A symbol-table lookup is not limited to the lexical-analysis phase.

title: Syntax-Directed Translation
subject: Compiler Design
cue: Attach semantic computations to grammar productions.
theory: Synthesized attributes flow from children toward a parent; inherited attributes receive context from parents or permitted siblings.
S-attributed definitions use only synthesized attributes. L-attributed definitions constrain inherited dependencies to support left-to-right evaluation.

recall.q: How can you check whether attributes have a valid evaluation order?
recall.a: Build their dependency graph and find a topological order; a cycle indicates a dependency problem.

pitfall: “Inherited” does not mean every sibling dependency is allowed.

title: Variable Scope
subject: Compiler Design
cue: Determine which declaration a name denotes.
theory: Static scope resolves a name through lexical program nesting; dynamic scope resolves through active caller environments.
Scope describes where a name can be used; lifetime describes when its object exists.

recall.q: Can an object outlive the local scope of a name referring to it?
recall.a: Yes, for example dynamically allocated storage or a static object.

pitfall: Do not confuse static scoping with static storage duration.

title: Viable Prefixes
subject: Compiler Design
cue: What may appear on a shift-reduce parser’s stack?
theory: A viable prefix is a prefix of a right-sentential form that does not extend beyond the right end of its handle.
The LR item automaton recognizes viable prefixes; goto transitions describe extending the stack’s recognized prefix.

recall.q: Why is “prefix of any sentence” too broad for viable prefix?
recall.a: A viable prefix is tied to a right-sentential form and must not pass the handle’s right end.

pitfall: A viable prefix may contain nonterminals, not only terminal input.

title: AVL Trees
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: A BST must remain height-balanced after updates.
theory: An AVL tree maintains a height difference of at most one between the two subtrees of every node.
LL/RR imbalance uses a single rotation; LR/RL uses a double rotation. Operations are O(log n).

recall.q: What information determines the rotation type?
recall.a: The unbalanced node and whether the heavy path turns left or right at its next step.

pitfall: A rotation must preserve inorder key order.

title: Abstract Data Types
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Separate allowed operations from their implementation.
theory: An ADT specifies values and operations by behavior, without fixing an array, list or other representation.
A stack ADT is LIFO whether implemented by an array or linked nodes.

recall.q: Is a linked list the only way to implement a queue?
recall.a: No. A circular array can implement the same queue ADT.

pitfall: Operation complexity depends on representation, not just the ADT name.

title: Arrays and Address Calculations
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Calculate element addresses or compare indexed access.
theory: For element size w and lower bound L, A[i] is at base+w(i−L).
A contiguous row-major 2D array stores all columns of one row before the next; the row stride is the number of columns times w.

recall.q: Which index varies fastest in row-major layout?
recall.a: The column index.

pitfall: Use the stated lower bounds and element size; a pointer is not the array’s total storage.

title: Binary Heaps
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Complete tree with min/max at the root.
theory: For a zero-indexed heap, children of i are 2i+1 and 2i+2; parent is floor((i−1)/2) for i>0.
The leaves occupy indices floor(n/2) through n−1. Bottom-up build-heap is Θ(n).

recall.q: How many leaves does an n-node binary heap have?

pitfall: Switching between 0-based and 1-based formulas changes every index.

title: Binary Search Trees
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Maintain ordered keys or analyze a BST search path.
theory: Inorder traversal returns sorted keys in a BST. Search/update costs O(h), with h depending on shape.
Deleting a two-child node commonly replaces it with its inorder predecessor or successor, then deletes that replacement node.

recall.q: Where is the inorder successor of a node with a right child?
recall.a: The leftmost node of its right subtree.

pitfall: A plain BST can degenerate into a chain.

title: Binary Trees
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Count binary-tree nodes or infer shape from traversals.
theory: At depth d there are at most 2ᵈ nodes. A height-h tree, counting edges, has at most 2ʰ⁺¹−1 nodes.
With distinct labels, inorder plus preorder or postorder determines the binary tree uniquely.

recall.q: For a nonempty binary tree, how are leaves and two-child nodes related?
recall.a: Number of leaves = number of two-child nodes + 1.

pitfall: State whether height counts edges or nodes.

title: Choosing a Data Structure
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Choose a structure from the required operations.
theory: A stack supports last-in-first-out access; a queue supports first-in-first-out access; a heap supports priority-based removal.
Choose using the mix of operations and costs, not one isolated favorable operation.

recall.q: Which structure naturally supports breadth-first search?
recall.a: A FIFO queue.

pitfall: Efficient insertion does not guarantee efficient searching.

title: Hashing
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Trace insertions and collisions in a table.
theory: Separate chaining stores a collection per bucket; open addressing stores keys within the table itself.
Follow the stated probe rule exactly and record occupied positions after every insertion.

recall.q: Can a chaining table have load factor greater than one?
recall.a: Yes; each bucket can hold multiple keys.

pitfall: A probe count may include the first slot; read the question’s convention.

title: Infix Prefix and Postfix
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Convert or evaluate infix, prefix or postfix expressions.
theory: In postfix evaluation, scan left to right: push operands, then pop the right operand before the left for a binary operator.
For infix conversion, an operator stack handles precedence, associativity and parentheses.

recall.q: For postfix “a b −”, which operand is subtracted from which?
recall.a: a−b: b is popped first as the right operand.

pitfall: Reversing pop order changes subtraction and division.

title: Linked Lists
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Pointer updates, reversal or insertion/deletion costs.
theory: A singly linked node stores data and a next pointer; indexed access requires traversal.
Insertion after a known node is O(1), while locating that node may take O(n).

recall.q: What must be saved before changing current.next during reversal?
recall.a: The original next node, so the remaining list is not lost.

pitfall: Deleting a node in a singly linked list generally requires its predecessor.

title: Priority Queues
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Repeatedly choose the most urgent or smallest item.
theory: A priority queue exposes an extreme key rather than FIFO order. A binary heap implements insertion and extract-extreme in O(log n).
Peek is O(1), while finding an arbitrary key in a heap can be O(n).

recall.q: Does equal arrival order determine removal order in a priority queue?
recall.a: Only if a tie-breaking rule explicitly preserves it.

pitfall: Priority queues and ordinary queues have different removal rules.

title: Queues
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: FIFO operations or circular-buffer indices.
theory: A queue inserts at the rear and removes from the front. A circular array reuses freed slots by modular indexing.
When front==rear is used for empty, full may need a count, a flag, or one deliberately unused slot.

recall.q: Why can a circular queue’s usable capacity be n−1?
recall.a: One slot may be reserved to distinguish full from empty.

pitfall: Use the implementation’s index convention, not a memorized full-condition formula.

title: Stacks
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Nested calls, parentheses or last-in-first-out order.
theory: A stack supports push, pop and top; a pop removes the most recently pushed remaining element.
Trace candidate output sequences with a stack to test whether a permutation is achievable.

recall.q: Why is a stack suited to matching nested parentheses?
recall.a: The most recently opened unmatched bracket must close first.

pitfall: Underflow occurs on an empty pop; overflow depends on the storage limit.

title: Data Structure Operation Costs
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Compare operation costs under a stated representation.
theory: Separate locating an element from modifying links or indices once it is known.
Worst-case, amortized and expected costs are different claims and require different assumptions.

recall.q: Why is dynamic-array append amortized O(1) despite occasional O(n) resizing?
recall.a: The total copying over many geometrically growing capacities is linear in the number of appends.

pitfall: One costly operation does not refute an amortized bound.

title: Trees
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: General tree identities or representations.
theory: An undirected tree with n vertices has n−1 edges and a unique simple path between every pair.
A connected graph with n−1 edges is a tree; deleting any tree edge disconnects it.

recall.q: Can a tree have a cycle?
recall.a: No; connectivity and acyclicity define an undirected tree.

pitfall: A rooted tree’s child counts are not the same as undirected degrees at nonroot nodes.

title: Tree Traversals
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Order nodes by preorder, inorder or postorder.
theory: Preorder visits the root first, postorder last, and inorder between the left and right subtrees.
An explicit stack can simulate recursive traversal; level-order uses a queue.

recall.q: Which traversal conveniently frees children before their parent?
recall.a: Postorder.

pitfall: Inorder is specifically defined for an ordered binary-tree setting.

title: Uniform Hashing Assumptions
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Estimate average bucket or probe behavior.
theory: Under simple uniform hashing, a key is equally likely to hash to any bucket; expected chaining length is α=n/m.
Expected chaining lookup takes Θ(1+α), including bucket access and scanning.

recall.q: What load factor keeps expected chaining operations constant?
recall.a: A load factor bounded by a constant, with suitable hashing assumptions.

pitfall: An average-case model does not prevent adversarial collisions.

title: C String Length and Pointer Difference
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: A character pointer advances until it finds a zero terminator.
theory: while (*b) b++ advances to the terminating zero in a valid C string. Subtracting the original pointer counts character elements traversed.
Reading a string literal is allowed. Modifying its characters is not; the source question’s function only reads and advances a local pointer.

recall.q: If b scans from the start of "abcd" to its terminator, what is b−a?
recall.a: 4, the number of characters before the terminator.

pitfall: The function requires a valid zero-terminated string; otherwise it may read outside the array.

title: Aliasing
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Different expressions may refer to one storage object.
theory: Aliasing means two references or pointers can access the same object; a write through one can affect reads through the other.
Trace object locations separately from pointer-variable values.

recall.q: If p and q point to the same int, what does *p=7 change?
recall.a: The shared int, so reading *q yields 7 while both pointers remain valid.

pitfall: Do not confuse changing p with changing *p.

title: Arrays in C
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Array-to-pointer conversion or multidimensional indexing.
theory: In most expressions, an array converts to a pointer to its first element; exceptions include sizeof and unary & on an array.
For int a[R][C], a+1 advances by one whole row, C integers.

recall.q: Why is sizeof(a) different from sizeof(p) when a is an array and p a pointer?
recall.a: The former measures the whole array object; the latter measures the pointer object.

pitfall: An array parameter declaration is adjusted to a pointer parameter.

title: Functions in C
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Calls, return values and parameter binding.
theory: C arguments are passed by value. A pointer value can be copied to let a function modify the pointed-to object.
Function arguments are not required to be evaluated left to right; precedence does not impose that order.

recall.q: Can assigning a new address to a local pointer parameter redirect the caller’s pointer?
recall.a: No. Pass a pointer to that pointer if the caller’s pointer object must change.

pitfall: Distinguish updating a parameter from updating the object it points to.

title: goto and Control Flow
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Execution jumps to a named label.
theory: C goto transfers control to a label in the same function; follow the target when tracing.
Unrestricted jumps make control-flow proofs and maintenance harder; they do not inherently imply slower code.

recall.q: Can goto jump to a label in a different function?
recall.a: No.

pitfall: A jump can bypass an initialization; verify an object has a valid value before using it.

title: Identify C Code Behavior
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Infer a routine’s result or side effects.
theory: Trace small inputs and give variables meaning: accumulated sum, scan position, count, or partial result.
Use a loop invariant or recurrence to extend the observed pattern to all permitted inputs.

recall.q: Why are return value and side effect separate?
recall.a: A function may return one value while modifying objects through pointers or globals.

pitfall: A plausible pattern from examples still needs reasoning about all iterations.

title: Loop Invariants
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Prove a loop computes the required result.
theory: An invariant holds at the chosen loop point before and after every completed iteration.
Combine the invariant with the exit condition to derive the postcondition, and separately justify termination.

recall.q: What are the invariant proof’s three checkpoints?
recall.a: Initialization, preservation and the conclusion at termination.

pitfall: An invariant alone can hold forever in a nonterminating loop.

title: C Output and Defined Behavior
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Find output or determine whether output is defined.
theory: First check types, lifetime, bounds and sequencing; only then calculate a numeric output.
In C11, unsequenced modifications of the same scalar object, or an unsequenced modification and conflicting read, can cause undefined behavior.

recall.q: Does operator precedence determine the order of all side effects?
recall.a: No; precedence determines grouping, while sequencing rules determine ordering.

pitfall: A program’s observed output on one compiler is not proof that the language defines it.

title: Parameter Passing in C
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Caller variables change after function calls.
theory: C uses call by value, including when the value is a pointer.
Changing *p changes the pointed-to object; assigning p changes only the function’s local pointer copy.

recall.q: How can a C function swap two caller integers?
recall.a: Receive pointers to them and swap the pointed-to values.

pitfall: Saying C “passes pointers by reference” is misleading; the pointer itself is passed by value.

title: Pointers
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Pointer arithmetic, dereferencing or declarations.
theory: p+k advances k elements of the pointed-to type, not k bytes unless p points to a one-byte character type.
Pointer arithmetic is valid within an array and one position past it; the one-past pointer must not be dereferenced.

recall.q: What is p[i] defined as?

pitfall: Pointer subtraction and ordering require the appropriate related-object conditions.

title: Programming Constructs
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Trace loops, conditionals and short-circuit operators.
theory: && and || evaluate left to right and skip the second operand when the result is already determined.
break exits the nearest enclosing loop or switch; continue proceeds to the next iteration of the nearest loop.

recall.q: For a for-loop, where does continue send control?
recall.a: To the loop’s iteration/update expression, then the condition check.

pitfall: break inside a switch nested in a loop exits the switch, not the loop.

title: Core C Semantics
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Mixed C rules involving arithmetic, control flow and storage.
theory: Track integer promotions and usual arithmetic conversions before performing mixed-type operations.
Integer division truncates toward zero in modern C; unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo one more than the type’s maximum value.

recall.q: Is signed integer overflow defined to wrap?
recall.a: No. Signed overflow is undefined behavior under ordinary C rules.

pitfall: Do not assume a particular integer size unless the problem states it.

title: Programming Paradigms
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Compare how languages organize computation.
theory: Imperative programs describe state-changing steps; functional programming emphasizes function evaluation; declarative styles describe required relationships.
A language can support multiple paradigms, and a programming paradigm is not an execution-speed guarantee.

recall.q: Is recursion exclusive to functional languages?
recall.a: No; imperative languages including C support it.

pitfall: A label such as “structured” does not mean a program contains no loops.

title: Recursion
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Nested calls, static locals or recursive output order.
theory: Each call has its own automatic local variables, while a static local has storage shared across calls.
Statements before the recursive call act on descent; statements after it act while calls return.

recall.q: Why do post-call prints often appear in reverse order?
recall.a: They execute as the call stack unwinds from deepest call to earliest caller.

pitfall: A static variable is not reset for each recursive call.

title: Object Lifetime and Runtime Storage
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Lifetime of automatic, static or dynamically allocated objects.
theory: Automatic objects normally live for their block activation; static-storage objects live for the program’s execution.
Allocated storage persists until freed, but all pointers to it become unusable for access after deallocation.

recall.q: Why is returning &local from a function unsafe?
recall.a: The automatic local object ends its lifetime when the function returns.

pitfall: A pointer variable can survive even though the object it points to has expired.

title: Strings
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Null termination, character arrays or string operations.
theory: A C string is a character sequence terminated by a zero character. strlen excludes that terminator.
A character array needs space for its contents plus the terminating zero; sizeof(array) measures the allocated array.

recall.q: Why can strlen(s) be smaller than sizeof(s)?
recall.a: The string may use only part of the array, and strlen stops at the first terminator.

pitfall: Modifying a string literal has undefined behavior.

title: Structures
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Member layout, padding or structure pointers.
theory: A struct stores all its members; padding may appear between members and at the end to satisfy alignment.
Use . for an object and -> for a pointer; p->x is equivalent to (*p).x.

recall.q: Is sizeof(struct) necessarily the sum of member sizes?
recall.a: No; alignment padding can increase it.

pitfall: Do not infer exact padding without the stated platform/layout rules.

title: switch and Fall-Through
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: A switch enters one label then may fall through.
theory: A switch transfers control to the matching case or default; without a match and without default, its body is skipped.
After entry, execution continues through later labels until break, return or the end; labels themselves do not stop fall-through.

recall.q: Do ordinary statements before the first case run on normal switch entry?
recall.a: No; dispatch jumps to a matching case/default label.

pitfall: Source notes claiming such statements “always execute” are incorrect.

correction.original: Statements before the first case label “will always execute.”
correction.corrected: On normal switch entry, control jumps to the matching case/default; ordinary statements before the first reached label are skipped.
correction.reason: C switch dispatch transfers control to a case/default label; see C11 draft §6.8.4.2, including its example.

title: Type Checking and Conversions
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Decide whether operands, assignments or calls have compatible types.
theory: Static type checking verifies type constraints before execution, but cannot establish every runtime property.
C permits some implicit conversions; a cast requests a conversion but does not make an invalid memory access safe.

recall.q: Does a successful compilation prove array accesses stay in bounds?
recall.a: No. Many bounds and lifetime errors are runtime semantic issues.

pitfall: A warning-free compilation is not a proof of defined behavior.

title: Unions
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Several members share one storage region.
theory: A union’s members overlap; its size must accommodate its largest member and required alignment.
Writing one member affects the shared representation, so reading another requires attention to C’s representation and type rules.

recall.q: How is a union different from a struct in storage?
recall.a: A union overlaps members; a struct reserves separate member regions.

pitfall: Do not add member sizes to compute a union size.

title: Variable Binding and Scope
subject: Programming and Data Structures
cue: Resolve a name to a declaration or object.
theory: C uses lexical scope; an inner declaration can hide an outer declaration with the same spelling.
Binding a name and allocating an object are distinct: scope, linkage and storage duration answer different questions.

recall.q: What happens to an outer variable when a same-named inner variable is declared?
recall.a: The outer object still exists, but its name is hidden in the inner scope.

pitfall: A static local’s long lifetime does not make its name visible everywhere.

title: Closure Properties
subject: Theory of Computation
cue: Combine languages using union, intersection or complement.
theory: Regular languages are closed under union, intersection, complement, concatenation and star.
CFLs are closed under union, concatenation, star and intersection with a regular language, but not general intersection or complement.

recall.q: If L is CFL and R is regular, what can you conclude about L∩R?
recall.a: It is context-free.

pitfall: Closure under union means finite/binary union here, not arbitrary infinite union. Nonclosure requires a counterexample, not failure for every pair.

title: Context-Free Grammars
subject: Theory of Computation
cue: Generate nested or recursively structured strings.
theory: In a CFG, each production has one nonterminal on the left and any string of symbols on the right.
A derivation replaces nonterminals until only terminals remain; a parse tree records the hierarchical replacements.

recall.q: What does S→aSb | ε generate?
recall.a: Exactly aⁿbⁿ for n≥0.

pitfall: A CFG may have many derivations of one tree; ambiguity requires distinct parse trees.

title: Context-Free Languages
subject: Theory of Computation
cue: One stack or a grammar may express the required dependency.
theory: CFLs are exactly the languages recognized by nondeterministic pushdown automata.
A single matched count such as aⁿbⁿ is context-free; aⁿbⁿcⁿ is not context-free.

recall.q: Are all regular languages also context-free?
recall.a: Yes. A PDA can simulate a finite automaton without using its stack.

pitfall: Two independent equal-count requirements may exceed one stack’s capability.

title: Countability and Diagonalization
subject: Theory of Computation
cue: Compare the number of strings, machines and languages.
theory: Over a finite nonempty alphabet, finite strings are countable; finite machine descriptions are therefore countable.
The set of all languages is the power set of the countably infinite string set, so it is uncountable.

recall.q: Why must some languages have no recognizing Turing machine?
recall.a: There are uncountably many languages but only countably many machine descriptions.

pitfall: A language can itself be a countable set of strings while belonging to an uncountable collection of languages.

title: Decidability
subject: Theory of Computation
cue: Ask whether an algorithm can always answer yes or no.
theory: A decider halts on every input. A recognizer must halt and accept members but may loop on nonmembers.
Rice’s theorem concerns nontrivial semantic properties of the recognized language, not every syntactic property of machine descriptions.

recall.q: Does undecidable mean no input instance can ever be solved?
recall.a: No; it means no algorithm correctly decides every instance while always halting.

pitfall: A finite simulation cannot generally prove that a machine will never halt.

title: Deterministic Pushdown Automata
subject: Theory of Computation
cue: A PDA must choose a unique next move.
theory: A DPDA has no competing enabled moves; an available ε-move must not compete with an input-consuming move for the same state and stack top.
Deterministic context-free languages form a proper subset of CFLs; nondeterminism increases PDA language power.

recall.q: Are DPDA and NPDA equally powerful?
recall.a: No. Some CFLs require nondeterministic pushdown recognition.

pitfall: Acceptance by final state and empty stack need special care for deterministic PDAs.

title: Finite Automata
subject: Theory of Computation
cue: Recognition needs only finite remembered information.
theory: A DFA has exactly one next state per state–symbol pair; an NFA may allow several or no moves and may use ε-transitions.
DFA and NFA recognize the same class: regular languages. A subset construction turns an NFA into a DFA.

recall.q: How does an NFA accept a string?
recall.a: At least one complete computation path consumes the string and ends in an accepting state.

pitfall: Acceptance is existential over paths; it does not require every path to accept.

title: Finite-State Machines with Output
subject: Theory of Computation
cue: A finite-state device produces outputs as input arrives.
theory: A Mealy machine associates output with transitions; a Moore machine associates output with states.
Trace the stated initial state and output convention, especially whether an initial output is produced before reading input.
To minimize a finite-state output machine, states may merge only when outputs agree appropriately and every input leads to equivalent successor states.

recall.q: Which model’s output depends directly on both current state and input symbol?
recall.a: Mealy.

pitfall: Output timing can differ even when two machines implement related behavior.

title: Classify a Language
subject: Theory of Computation
cue: Choose the weakest language class that suffices.
theory: Try finite memory first; use a stack for nesting or one unbounded last-in-first-out dependency.
To disprove a class, use a valid pumping argument, closure reduction, or a distinguishability argument; failed intuition is not a proof.

recall.q: Is every language accepted by a PDA nonregular?
recall.a: No. Every regular language can also be accepted by a PDA.

pitfall: An upper bound such as “context-free” does not prove the language is not regular.

title: Regularity of Symbol-Count Conditions
subject: Theory of Computation
cue: Compare languages defined by counts of symbols.
theory: Finite conditions such as count modulo k can be recognized with finitely many states.
Exact equality of two unbounded counts can require unbounded memory; test the actual language rather than the appearance of a formula.

recall.q: Can a DFA track the number of a’s modulo 3?
recall.a: Yes, using three remainder states.

pitfall: The book’s “Medium” is a difficulty tag, not a theory topic.

correction.original: The note interprets “Medium” as computational models.
correction.corrected: “Medium” is a difficulty tag. The associated question belongs to regular-language classification.
correction.reason: The single associated question on page 371 is GATE CSE 2006 Q29, asking which symbol-count language is not regular.

title: DFA Minimization
subject: Theory of Computation
cue: Find the minimum DFA or merge equivalent states.
theory: Remove unreachable states, separate accepting from rejecting states, and refine partitions by transition behavior.
Two states are distinguishable if some suffix leads to acceptance from one and rejection from the other.

recall.q: What does Myhill–Nerode count for a regular language?
recall.a: The distinct right-congruence classes, equal to the number of states in its minimal complete DFA.

pitfall: An n-state NFA may require up to 2ⁿ DFA states; it does not always require exactly 2ⁿ.

title: Nondeterminism
subject: Theory of Computation
cue: Several computation paths are possible.
theory: An NFA accepts if any path succeeds; subset construction tracks the entire set of reachable NFA states after each prefix.
Nondeterminism preserves finite-automaton and Turing-machine language power, but increases pushdown-automaton power.

recall.q: Do you choose one arbitrary NFA branch when constructing its DFA?
recall.a: No. Each DFA state represents all currently possible NFA states.

pitfall: Take ε-closures when the NFA includes ε-transitions.

title: Counting Automaton States
subject: Theory of Computation
cue: Bound or prove an automaton’s state count.
theory: A state summarizes information about the prefix needed for future acceptance decisions.
A lower bound follows by producing prefixes that are pairwise distinguishable using suitable suffixes.

recall.q: What must differ between two prefixes to require different DFA states?
recall.a: Some common suffix must make one resulting string accepted and the other rejected.

pitfall: A proposed construction gives an upper bound; minimality needs a lower-bound argument.

title: Pumping Lemmas
subject: Theory of Computation
cue: Prove a language nonregular or not context-free.
theory: Regular pumping: for sufficiently long w, some w=xyz has |xy|≤p, |y|>0, and xyⁱz∈L for every i≥0.
For a nonregularity proof, choose w after p is fixed, then defeat every allowed split; you may choose the pumping exponent after seeing the split.
CFL pumping uses w=uvxyz with |vxy|≤p and |vy|>0, requiring uvⁱxyⁱz∈L for every i≥0. Both pumped pieces use the same exponent.

recall.q: Can satisfying the pumping lemma prove regularity?
recall.a: No. It is necessary, not sufficient. Construct an automaton or regex to prove regularity.

pitfall: You cannot choose only one convenient split when disproving regularity.

title: Pushdown Automata
subject: Theory of Computation
cue: Use a stack for matching, nesting or reversed comparison.
theory: A PDA reads input and updates a stack based on current state and stack top. NPDAs recognize exactly CFLs.
The stack naturally reverses stored information, making balanced nesting and aⁿbⁿ natural examples.

recall.q: Why can a PDA recognize aⁿbⁿ?
recall.a: Push for each a, then pop for each b, checking that the counts and order match.

pitfall: An unrestricted second stack would increase power to that of a Turing machine.

title: Decidable and Recognizable Languages
subject: Theory of Computation
cue: Distinguish recognizers from always-halting deciders.
theory: A recursive language has a decider; a recursively enumerable language has a recognizer that may loop on nonmembers.
L is recursive exactly when both L and its complement are recursively enumerable.

recall.q: Why can two recognizers decide L when one recognizes L and the other its complement?
recall.a: Run them in interleaved steps; exactly one must eventually accept.

pitfall: Running one recognizer to completion before starting the other can hang forever.

title: Reductions
subject: Theory of Computation
cue: Transfer undecidability using an instance transformation.
theory: A mapping reduction A≤mB is a total computable function f with x∈A exactly when f(x)∈B.
If A is undecidable and A≤mB, then B is undecidable: a decider for B would decide A.

recall.q: Which direction proves a new problem B hard?
recall.a: Reduce a known hard problem A to B, not B to A.

pitfall: The transformation must halt and preserve yes/no membership.

title: Regular Expressions
subject: Theory of Computation
cue: Describe languages using union, concatenation and repetition.
theory: Regular expressions use union, concatenation and Kleene star; they characterize exactly regular languages.
Kleene star includes zero repetitions, so ε∈L* even if L is empty.

recall.q: What is ∅*?

pitfall: ∅ and {ε} are different languages.

title: Regular Grammars
subject: Theory of Computation
cue: Translate a one-sided linear grammar to an automaton.
theory: A standard right-linear grammar has rules like A→aB, A→a and optionally A→ε. Such grammars generate regular languages.
Nonterminals can serve as automaton states, with terminal-labeled transitions following productions.

recall.q: Can right-linear and left-linear rules be mixed arbitrarily while guaranteeing regularity?
recall.a: No. The grammar must obey a consistent regular-grammar form.

pitfall: A CFG being linear is not enough to guarantee it is regular.

title: Regular Languages
subject: Theory of Computation
cue: Check whether finite memory is sufficient.
theory: A language is regular exactly when some DFA, NFA or regular expression describes it.
All finite languages are regular; an infinite language can also be regular, such as a*.

recall.q: Does infinite length range imply nonregularity?
recall.a: No. A loop in a finite automaton handles arbitrarily long strings.

pitfall: “Needs counting” is too vague: bounded or modular counting is finite-state.

title: Turing Machines
subject: Theory of Computation
cue: General computation with read/write tape memory.
theory: A Turing machine has finite control and unbounded tape; a recognizer may not halt on every input.
Multitape and nondeterministic TMs have the same recognizable-language power as standard deterministic TMs, though efficiency can differ.

recall.q: Does a Turing machine’s existence for L imply L is decidable?
recall.a: Only if it is guaranteed to halt on every input with the correct answer.

pitfall: Computability equivalence does not imply identical running time.
